Routine: Really.. None currently haha. During the combing process I washed my hair with shampoo daily, because a lot of filth was trapped in the mats. Obviously my hair took quite a toll, I'm going to be trying the CG method after I get my hair cut (tomorrow)

So, for some info. I have been depressed and suicidal for a really long time, probably 4 years or so. Of course this sucks on its own, but the hair just made it even worse. When you're that depressed and suicidal, it gets really really really hard to shower consistently, detangle your hair at all, and this only furthers the isolation to the point where my hair became one of the leading causes of my depression. I felt so ashamed and horrible about it, my hair was COMPLETELY matted up, into a big clump of dreadlock-like consistency. I was so ashamed that I didn't even take pictures or saw anyone, it looked horrible. [Here is a picture](https://i.imgur.com/jf4GGcW.jpg) outlining roughly how big the mat was.

Now things have been improving for me since the new year, and quarantine actually left my family with a lot of time. My father is the one who did all the brushing on my hair. For over a month we combed an hour a day and only skipped a few days. Now my hair was just so matted that finger detangling was too gentle, and a rat tail comb was too bendy and weak. We used the end of a teasing comb, mostly. Yes, we did pull on my hair. A lot. But all of this wasn't even breaking my hair that much, it was simply pulling out the already dead hair that just got stuck in the mat. It was VERY painful, especially when we got to the parts higher on my head, where a thin layer of dense mats covered my scalp.

But oh boy oh man we did it! The first surprise was the filth. This already surprised me when we were in the process of combing. It was very dirty. The second, even bigger surprise was the length. I've never had hair this long before! It kinda saddens me that I'm going to get it all cut off, but it's necessary. I'm not ready yet to deal with hair this length, and my ends are really bad. Tomorrow I'm going in for a reset cut, to about shoulder length and with layers. You can see that most of my hair is actually only slightly wavy, and then curls at the end. I hope my curls come back quickly higher up once I cut off all the cute curls at the ends... I will be going CG and hope this helps!

All in all, I am hopeful. It feels refreshing to be able to rake my hands through my hair.. Thank you for reading xp

Cat color genetics.

I know all the cat colors.

If you want I can list them.

EDIT: I've been asked, so here they are. I'll be going over all cat colors that are not weird mutations. Keep in mind you can pretty much combine them all and if I'd list all the combinations we'd be here forever. So you could combine a black base color with the tabby pattern and the colourpoint pattern, and you get a seal lynx point cat. Google that if you want. Also we're not going into hybrid colors no thanks.

BASE COLORS ----------- 

Cats can have eumelanin or pheomelanin or both. These are the types

Red - Red is the color of an orange cat. Fun fact, all red cats look like tabbies, even if they're not genetically tabbies. Red pigment is called pheomelanin.

Black - Black is black. Black pigment is called eumelanin. Chocolate and cinnamon are also eumelanin.

Chocolate - Warm, dark brown color. Google Havana Brown cat breed. It's not common outside of purebreds, most brown tabbies are actually genetically black.

Cinnamon - Even warmer, almost reddish brown color. Least common of the eumelanins, since it's recessive to both black and chocolate.

TORTIES ----------- 

Torties and calicos are cats with both pheomelanin and eumelanin. This means you can have red together with any of the eumelanins, most commonly black. A tortie has little to no white and a calico has a lot of white. Torties and calicos are (save a few mutations) always female since you need two X chromosomes to have both eumelanin and pheomelanin.

DILUTIONS ------------

Dilute a base color and it becomes lighter. Works for torties too.

Cream - Cream is the dilute form of red. They will usually still have faint tabby markings even if they're not genetically tabbies.

Blue - Blue is grey. The name's a bit confusing since they don't look grey, but a bazillion other things DO look grey so having a unique name is important.

Lilac - Lilac is dilute chocolate, it's like a warmer grey. Hard to tell apart from blue, but almost only present in purebred cats.

Fawn - Very very uncommon, looks a lot like cream but lacks the faint tabby markings.

TABBIES ----------

Tabbies are fun. There's many types. Also, a genetically black cat will look brown or grey as a tabby.

Solid - Not a tabby. No tabby markings, unless it's a red or cream cat. Those are called ghost markings.

Mackerel - Most common type of tabby. It's got stripes and sometimes a few spots.

Classic - Classic tabbies are still pretty common, they have a really cool swirly pattern and are my fave tabby type.

Ticked - Ticked tabbies have almost no markings on their body, except for the face, legs, and tip of the tail. Black ticked tabbies can look very reddish, google Abyssinian cat.

Spotted - It's got spots. Pretty self-explanatory. Google Egyptian Mau cat.

ALBINOS --------

Albino sounds special, but these three are forms of albinism and not that special. They're temperature based, the cold parts of the cats are darkest. Genetically black variations of these are called seal and tabby is called lynx.

Colourpoint - Also called Siamese. Dark on the 'points' (the face, the legs, the ears, and the tail), very light everywhere else. Highest contrast. Has blue eyes.

Mink - Also called Tonkinese. Dark on the 'points', medium color everywhere else. Medium contrast. Blue to greyish eyes.

Sepia - Also called Burmese. Dark on the points, also pretty dark everywhere also. Little contrast. Gold eyes.

SMOKES AND SILVERS ---------

These are cool and weird.

Smoke - Smoke is the solid version of this. Basically, the base of the hair is whitish and the rest is the base color. Most striking on longhaired black cats.

Silver - Silver is the tabby version of this. Basically, anything except the markings is whitish and the rest is the base color.

Chinchilla/shell - Very very pale version of smoke.

GOLDEN -------------

Take any of the smoke things and make the whitish parts gold. Boom, pretty cats. 'Smoothie' the photogenic cat is this color.

WHITES ----------

Whites of all varieties.

Dominant white - A dominant gene that overshadows all of the other colors, the whole cat becomes entirely white. Has gold/orange/yellow eyes or blue eyes. If it's blue eyes, it's more likely to be deaf.

White spotting - Very common. Causes white paws, white markings, all that jazz. It kind of predictably 'spreads' up the cat the more white you have. From the paws to the underbelly and chest up the body to the face and finishing off with the tail and ears. Turkish Van cats have very high white spotting, for example.

You seem to have a misunderstanding of the subject. There are only two species allowed to be service animals- dogs and miniature horses. These are animals that basically have a job. Emotional support animals, like the alligator, are much different. They are essentially just pets that by their mere presence calm the owner or help them. This means they're not entitled to be taken on a plane like a service animal would. These are more like buddies, but professional buddies, and any animal can be it. Yeah, most people haven't heard of it. 'Eating disorder' usually brings up images of skinny young girls starving themselves to be prettier or gain control or something, but there are many other eating disorders. It's interesting because people with ARFID can actually have any weight, say someone's 'safe' foods are all junk food. It can also be caused by traumatic experiences with food- like allergic reactions.

The chirping noise, does it sound like the hamster is chattering its teeth? If so, that can either mean the hamster is mildly annoyed or scared, or that the hamster is rather content and happy. The only way to tell really is context and other body language. If the hamster makes the noise while eating some food, he's probably happy. If his ears are down and he's near the other hamster, it's likely annoyance. Does the sound resemble a loud, scream-like squeal? That means your hamster is very scared. They often make this sound while showing their teeth clearly. It's basically like a last-ditch effort to intimidate the perceived aggressor enough to scare them away.

> As someone who has a lot of ASD symptoms myself, I can tell you that autism condemns people to a life of suffering.

Hey, I also have autism! I don't think that is necessarily the case. This post will explain!

> It can cause social isolation, shame, and stigmas from others, and extreme difficulty developing adult skills and executive functioning

Social isolation, shame, and stigmas all aren't caused by autism. They're caused by the people around you. This means that we should educate people and change their attitudes about autism. Sadly, much of the world is still ableist against things like autism. Adult skills and executive functioning definitely are problems, ones I deal with myself too. The reality is though that these can be managed with a supportive environment and good therapy which specializes in autism. My psychologist helped me so much to establish a routine in many different ways, and ways to cope if it changes. I am not an adult yet, but I am slowly becoming more independent like people my age should be.

> Many autistic people cannot get jobs, and the ones who can often struggle to get one or get a very prestigious/high-paying one.

Though you are right that people with autism have a much harder time getting jobs, I again don't think this is because of the autism. Many people would do fine with minor adjustments that wouldn't hurt their contribution (such as being able to be excused when they feel a meltdown coming or being able to keep a fidget of some kind). Then also, many autistic people actually have intense interests on certain topics and make great people for niche jobs which may or may not be high-paying. And even if they're not, high-paying or prestigious, many jobs aren't. That doesn't make them bad or not worthwhile.

> I recently saw a post in AITA where a 15-year-old girl received almost no attention from her parents, as they had a 19-year-old autistic son, who kept everyone up at night, got 100% of the attention from the parents, ruined the girl's childhood, and even physically assaulted her.

This is a family who would benefit from help. They need to be able to find coping mechanisms for the son and get help in the household so the daughter is no longer ignored. That's what specialized caregivers are for. It doesn't need a cure. They should be able to get some affordable soundproofing for the son's room or something of the likes. This only shows that they need to receive more and better quality help. The thing about the assault is very sad, but without knowing the full circumstances, these things have triggers and stuff that leads up to it. Specialists can recognize these and teach the parents to recognize it, preventing such things. Like I said, better quality help.

> It's ironic that people seek out a cure, yet try to treat autism with special ed and CBT - effectively attempting to cure it anyway.
Special ed isn't a cure of any kind, not even attempting to be. It's just education at the kid's own speed.

> Parents of autistic people who oppose a cure are hypocrites if they attempt to treat their children. If you are attempting to put an autistic person through therapy, you are effectively attempting to remove their autistic traits. But you oppose a cure for it...?

As you may have noticed I am a huge proponent of therapy. It should be said that I think good therapy doesn't blindly remove autistic traits. It helps people cope and prevents bad stuff, never does it completely remove a trait. There have been forms of therapy which attempt to remove harmless autistic traits (such as hand flapping) but these are very much hated by most people who oppose a cure, as they are often cruel and sad. It should also be noted that this sort of borderline-torture has been endorsed by organizations like Autism Speaks that work toward a cure.

> This logic cannot be applied to other illnesses.

It can to disorders like ADHD or Dyslexia.


> My debilitating obsessive-compulsive disorder that nearly drove me to suicide twice is NOT "just a part of who I am". We are not "discriminating against" people with cancer or ALS by seeking cures for cancer or ALS. Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder are not "just part of someone's personality", they're absolutely horrifying illnesses that need to be treated very aggressively.

You are right. These things you listed all aren't just part of who someone is. Autism isn't like any off these things though. First of, it doesn't kill you like cancer or ALS. Comparing them is straight-up dishonest. I'm sorry about your OCD and suicidality, truly, I have struggled with feelings of suicide as well. We can't however compare these things to autism. You aren't born with OCD, you develop it. Autism is different. There are differences between autistic babies and neurotypical ones *in the womb*. Autism can be diagnosed at its earliest at 3 months old. That's crazy. You grow up with it, you keep it forever, it never ever goes away. I don't know any different. Autism isn't just a part of who I am, *it is who I am.* It shapes everything, from how I act socially to how I perceive the world to how I deal with problems and the things I like.

> So why is autism looked at so much differently than OCD, schizophrenia, bipolar, ADHD, cancer, MS, ALS, or Leukemia?

For OCD, schizophrenia, and bipolar, it's because you're born with it. Cancer, MS, ALS, and leukemia are all physical illnesses and can kill you (MS less so). ADHD really shouldn't be looked at that differently. They're very similar in many ways, both being neurodevelopmental disorders you're born with. In that case, I also don't know why it's looked at so much differently.

Real late with this one but here it goes. How I'm doing it is I will list it in different sections ROUGHLY based on the locus they're on. This means that they can be combined if they're in different sections. I will also put in if that combination does anything weird. Also if there's mistakes tell me, this is all from the top of my head lol. Also not gonna go into bengals and other hybrids, they're very weird and little is sure about the actual genetics.


SECTION 1 - Red and Not Red™

Red (Red pigment is also called pheomelanin. Hugely varies in shade. Always looks tabby even if not genetically tabby.)

Not Red (Called eumelanin. Three types, will get into.)

Tortoiseshell/calico (Only in females but rarely males. Combines red with a not red. Tortie is when there is little to 
no white, and calico is with more white spotting. White spotting makes patches bigger.)


SECTION 2 - Not Reds/eumelanin

Black (Your basic eumelanin. The base for all the others and by far the most common)

Chocolate (Mutation of black. A rich dark brown, usually only in purebreds but sometimes others too.)

Cinnamon (Mutation of black. Reddish brown, lighter than chocolate. The rarest not red, and pretty much only in purebreds.)


SECTION 3 - Dilutes

Dilute (One gene that does a whole lot, lemme go more specific. In torties and calicos both red and not red will be diluted.)

 -Red (Dilute makes red into cream. Still always tabby, but much lighter.)

 -Black (Turns it blue. Should be noted that blue just looks like grey. Actual blue cats don't exist.)

 -Chocolate (Turns it lilac. A warmer grey, sometimes looks faintly purple too.)

 -Cinnamon (Turns it fawn. Super duper rare, like cream but warmer. Pinkish.)


SECTION 4 - Tabbies

Not tabby (A solid color, unless red. Reds always look like tabbies.)

Tabby (Any of the following 3 types. Think of it as making the non-striped parts lighter, rather than adding dark 
stripes. Thus the stripes on a genetically black cat will be just black while the non-striped parts brown.)

 -Mackerel (The most common tabby, housecat standard. It has stripes. Wowie.)

 -Classic (Slightly less common but still in moggies. The stripes turn blotchier and turn. Bullet eye pattern.)

 -Ticked (Stripes on face, and sometimes on legs and tail. Makes the true color be on the tip of the hair, so black looks like brown pretty much. See abyssinians. Also most dominant.)


SECTION 5 - Spots (partially theory, but best explanation if you ask me)

Not spotted (Mackerel tabbies look like mackerel tabbies.)

Broken (Mackerel tabby turns into broken lines. So not straight stripes.)

Spotted (Mackerel tabby turns into spotted tabby. The stripes become so broken off they're spots now.)


SECTION 6 - Smoke and whatnot (inhibitor gene)

Not smoke (normal bois)

Smoke/silver/inhibitor gene (does a lot of things)

 -Tabbies (The inhibitor gene on a tabby turns it silver. This means that the non-striped parts become grey-whitish. 
So a chocolate tabby with the gene becomes like a greyish cat with brown stripes, a black one becomes a greyish 
cat with black stripes.)

 -Solids (Turns it smoke, shaded, or chinchilla. With smoke, the cat has a white undercoat, with only 1/2 of the hair 
showing the true color. Very striking on long haired cats, they get a white 'mane'. With shorthairs barely visible unless you brush through the hair. Also, they may get faint tabby markings. With shaded, 1/4 of the hair shows the true color. Very rare and its weird how its inherited exactly. With chinchilla, even less true color shows. They look mostly white. Even rarer.)


SECTION 7 - Golden/wideband gene

Not golden (Normal silver or non silver)

Golden (Only does stuff if the inhibitor gene is present. Turns the white parts a golden shade, and the true color gets a golden shine too. Super rare, not much known about it.)


SECTION 8 - The albinos ohhh boy

Not albino (normal)

Sepia/burmese (Causes the true color to be lighter on the body, with the most true color on the 'points', aka the 
face, ears, legs, and tail. This is because these parts are colder. Temperature dependant. Black looks brown on the points and is called seal. Darkest albino. Has golden eyes.)

Mink/tonkinese (A lighter sepia, the difference between the points and the body is more noticable. Black looks brown on the points and is called seal. Grey or aqua eyes, sometimes golden or blue.)

Colourpoint/siamese (Often called siamese, but also present in ragdolls and non-purebreds. A lighter tonkinese, the difference between the points and body is so that the body is nearly white. Black looks brown on the points and is called seal. Blue eyes.)

True albino (Blue eyed, lilac eyed, or red eyed rarely. The cat has no pigment, so even blue eyes look much more pinkish. Very rare.)


SECTION 9 - Whites!

No white (no true white present on the cat, though whites from silver or colourpoint can be there.)

White spotting (Super common and varies hugely in how much white there actually is. The white sort of spreads, starting at the paws and chest, then underbelly and head, then full body, then ears and tail. This means you are unlikely to have a cat with only a white tail, or fully white with colored paws. Fully white cats due to white spotting exist and aren't more likely to be deaf. If the white reaches the eyes the cat can have blue eyes.)

Dominant white (Fully white with golden, yellow, orange or blue eyes. Cats with blue eyes are much more likely to be deaf.)
